utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Tom Hannis, and Jasmina Bosnjakovic for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence. Our client is not present. He already signed a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And are we ready to have the witness escorted in?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one small matter before we start with the witness. We received last night the new version of witness statement with annexes totalling some 87 pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In respect of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I didn't even have the time to read it, let alone analyse it, so we will not be able to start the cross-examination of this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, maybe I can give some background into this. During the last couple days of proofing, the witness made some revisions, alterations, additions to the annexes attached to her 2 June 2010 statement. The size of what we disclosed to the Defence yesterday is deceptive. It's -- looks worse than it really is. Rather than having the standard addendum that we submit with a 92 ter package that results from proofing, where you would list a particular line in the statement and indicate the change, so you would cross-reference the two documents, as a practical solution because that would require a lot of work for the Trial Chamber and the Defence to flip between the addendum and the original annexes, we inserted all the changes, all the revisions, into the annexes and produced revised annexes. So we really saw that as a practical solution to make it easier for them to read. Now, we turned over this morning red-lined versions of the changes to the annexes so the Defence can review them. Two points. It's important to know what materials is in the annexes. This is simply her results of her review of the log-books, in other words, the cases she was able to identify that fall within either one of the annexes -- one of the schedules to the indictment or she concluded involved serious crimes committed by Serb perpetrators against non-Serb victims between April and December of 1992. So really, her annexes can be looked at along with the log-books themselves to verify the information she found, and Defence could either agree that she found the relevant cases or that she missed some. I also want to note that the vast majority of the revisions are really in favour of the Defence; in other words, she identified some additional cases that the police reported to the prosecutor's offices that fall either within the scope of the indictment or involved serious crimes against non-Serbs. And I believe that once the Defence have taken a look at these revisions, they're not going to have a strong objection to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, why am I sitting here thinking that having regard to everything that you have just said that it is surprising that at some point between yesterday evening when this material was forwarded to the Defence and the point at which the Judges took the bench this morning that counsel on both sides would have had a chat about this as to what the consequence of this is in terms of the time, allocation of time, and how we are proceeding today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, well the witness was reviewing the annexes up until about 7.00, 7.30 last night, and then we had to get them into the system and disclosed as quickly as possible. So I didn't have time last evening to talk with the Defence. I did talk with Mr. Zecevic and the Zupljanin Defence this morning and they did indicate their concerns, and I explained really what these annexes contain and what the revisions consist of. So we communicated at that stage. I suggested that we do something similar with Mr. Vasic, Witness ST-210, which is perhaps take a slightly extended break after I do my examination-in-chief. The Defence can take a look at the revisions and see whether it really is necessary for them to delay the cross-examination. The witness wanted me to sit in on their proofing which occurred on Sunday, and I note that I didn't see much of what they were raising that dealt directly with the annexes themselves. So perhaps once they've seen the revisions, see that they're not really detrimental to their case, they might be in a position where they say, Well, we can go ahead with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is Mr. Olmsted being unduly optimistic in his proposal, that an extended break after he has completed his examination-in-chief may resolve the concerns that you think you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid so, Your Honours, my concerns are -- I would like to state that my concerns are basically objective concerns because I didn't even have time to read the -- this additional statement with the annexes, with the revised annexes, let alone analyse it. Therefore, I would, at the very least, need to be able to analyse it once before I could give you any information which would be -- which could be regarded as a solid information about that. So in that sense, I don't see that it is achievable -- that the suggestion which Mr. Olmsted made would be achievable or realistic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm going to, of course, take the views of my fellow Judges, but I am thinking that the most efficient course would be that the -- at the conclusion of the examination-in-chief we come back after the usual time, after the usual break, and then counsel would report as to whether we should take an extended break -- pick up the hearing at a later point in the course of today. Let me confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So that is the course that we will follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought in, may I take the usual practice in giving a brief summary of what is contained within this witness's 92 ter package. As background, Ms. Gacinovic was appointed deputy basic prosecutor in Trebinje in 1976 and held that position until August 1992, when she was appointed higher prosecutor for Trebinje, a position she has held ever since, although the title has changed over time. As Your Honours know, the Trebinje higher prosecutor's office had jurisdiction over two municipalities charged in the indictment: Gacko and Bileca. At the request of the ICTY Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Gacinovic reviewed the prosecutor office log-books from the period of 1992 through 1995, covering the 20 municipalities charged in the indictment as well as the higher prosecutor's office log-books to the extent those log-books were still existing. As the Trial Chamber has heard from other witnesses, these offices consisted of -- these log-books consisted of a KT log-book which contained criminal reports of known perpetrators, KTN log-books which contained criminal reports of unknown perpetrators' crimes, and then a KTA log-book which included on-site investigation reports filed by the courts as well as other official notes that really weren't criminal reports per se. Now, in reviewing these log-books, Ms. Gacinovic was asked to address essentially three issues. The first was whether any of the crimes listed in the schedules to the indictment are recorded in the log-books; second, the extent to which the log-books record criminal reports of serious crimes committed by Serb perpetrators against non-Serb victims between 1 April and 31 December 1992; and finally, to provide some statistical information about the number and kinds of cases that the prosecutor offices received in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we have the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Good morning to you, ma'am. The first thing I would point out --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- is that the solemn declaration that you have made exposes to the pain of the penalties of perjury which this Tribunal is by its constituent Statute and power to impose should you give false or misleading testimony. With that I would ask you, first of all, to tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Slobodanka Gacinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And could you summarise your professional background for us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completed primary school at Danilovgrad, Montenegro, and I graduated from secondary school in Ginozija [phoen], Trebinje 1969. I graduated from the faculty of law at the university of Belgrade in 1974 in February 1974. In October, I got a job at the primary school and preschool education centre in Trebinje as a secretary. Until December 1975 I worked there, and then I got a job with the basic public prosecutor's office at Trebinje. I was an intern until May 1976. In June, I passed the bar exam and I was elected to be a deputy basic prosecutor in Trebinje. I held that position until August 1982, when I was appointed higher public prosecutor in Trebinje. I was in that position until March 2004. Then my title changed when I was elected chief district prosecutor in Trebinje. Last year I was -- my term in office was extended and I still remain in the same position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in any of the countries that comprise the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some ten years or so ago I appeared as a witness in a case where we conducted an investigation -- actually, it was the investigating judge of the basic court in Trebinje. In that case I was heard as a witness, but I didn't testify before any other court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, in this case you have been called by the Prosecution, and under an expedited procedure permitted by the Rules of the Tribunal the Prosecution would be examining you for only 20 minutes. After that you would be cross-examined, of course as you would expect, by counsel for each of the other accused -- each of the two accused and the times that they have indicated subject to some variation that may have occurred in the course of -- since it was first indicated is a total of three hours and it was expected that your testimony would have been completed within the compass of today's sitting which ends at 1.45. The usual pattern is that the court takes a break after no longer than an hour and a half to allow for the technical changing of tapes and also the comfort of counsel and the witnesses and everyone else. But that may be varied today. But notwithstanding those fixed periods, if at any time you need to take a break you will indicate that to the Court, and we will, of course, accommodate you. And I would of course invite Mr. Olmsted to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My recollection may be incorrect, but I believe I was granted 30 minutes to examine her. It was an oral ruling. I'll tell you what I want to do, it's quite simple other than doing the standard questions with regard to the 92 ter package, I want to take the Trial Chamber through one of her annexes so that you'll be able to review it on your own and make a couple of clarifications so that when you see something perhaps you'll understand what she meant by it. And then I just wanted to ask her some more general questions about things she observed through her review of these log-books and I think I can do that within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't pretend to remember this, Mr. Olmsted, but I take you at your word, so 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Gacinovic. Now, prior to testifying today, did you have the opportunity to review your written statements from 2 June 2010 and 28 July 2010?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the 2 June 2010 statement, did you have some corrections and clarifications to some of the annexes to that statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter 10530 on the screen and I also want to hand the witness a copy of her addendum. And while they're bringing that up, just to note for the record since this was produced yesterday, we did not have the opportunity to insert the ERN numbers onto it. That will be done very soon, it was just in the process of getting that done. We'll have that done before we seek to tender it. I'm actually interested for the -- on the screen if we can have the -- there we go. Now it's on the screen to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Ms. Gacinovic, can you just confirm that this is the addendum to your 2 June statement containing the 11 annexes you revised during proofing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: With these revisions to the annexes, are you satisfied that the information contained in your written statements is accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to show you one of the revised annexes by way of an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can have page 32 of the original, of the B/C/S, and page 15 of the English on the screen. This is the revised annex 8 which applied to the Teslic office of the prosecutor's log-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want you to first -- and you can look at the one in front of you if that's easier, but it's also on the screen. And I want you to first -- do you have it in front of you, Ms. Gacinovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: I have reviewed it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if we can first look at -- under issue number 1 we see that you recorded one criminal case that you determined falls within the schedules B7, C7, and D7 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And for the record, this is the Mici group case which the Trial Chamber has already heard evidence on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Ms. Gacinovic, do you recall, other than this case, how many other cases you found in the log-books you reviewed that pertained to issue 1; in other words, crimes charged in the schedules of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: I subsequently identified four more cases that referred to the indictment in this case against Mico Stanisic, against Stojan Zupljanin, as is mentioned under item 1 of this table of the annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And we have this one in front of us which is Teslic. There was one for Vogosca, is that correct, and then there was one for --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one for Vogosca and two for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well. And those can be found in revised annex 5 and revised annex 15 and they pertain to incidents charged in the schedules under D16-1, B1-2, and B6-1. Now, if we could turn the page, page 34 in the original and page 19 in the English, we see issue 2 which are cases of serious crimes committed by Serb perpetrators against non-Serb victims between 1 April and 31 December 1992 that you were able to identify in the various log-books that you reviewed. And before we go through this issue I want to turn quickly to 65 ter 10528, and I want to turn to page 14 of the B/C/S and page 8 of the English. And, Ms. Gacinovic, can you confirm that this is the list of serious crimes that you were asked to identify under issue 2?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, looking at this list were there any crimes on this list that you did not focus on when reviewing the log-books?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Article 172 of the Criminal Code of the RS is referred to here under item 4, but I didn't focus on that so much because I focused on Article 187 [as interpreted] of the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the consequences of the crime committed because Article 187 stipulates serious bodily injury or great damage done to property.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify for the record, we have it on our transcript that you're referring to Article 187. Is it 187 or 177 that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: 177 is the article of the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly, Article 172 does not involve instances where there is serious physical injury to a victim involved in the crime?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the basic offence. When serious danger to lives or property is caused, and Article 177 when there is serious bodily injury or great damage to property or the lethal outcome of an injury. But I mostly focused on Article 177 which actually comprises the basic offence as described in Article 172.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have 65 ter 10530 back on the screen, page 34 of the original, page 16 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the entries under issue number 2, we see that in the last two columns you provide information regarding the date when the indictment was filed in the particular case, and in the last column the resolution of the case. Now, for some of the entries in your annexes, one or both of these columns are blank. For example, if we look at the first entry under issue 2 we see that the date of indictment for the first entry is not -- is blank. Can you explain what -- how should we interpret the blanks on these -- in these annexes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, KT177/72, the SJB in Teslic submitted a criminal report to the prosecutor's office in Teslic, a report against Mile Stanojevic. The victim was Fadil Resulovic. The crime was committed on the 5th of August, 1992, so this was in the period between April until the end of 1992. The crime here is 148/1, and looking at the log-books we can see that the indictment was not issued but rather the investigation was halted in 1993, which in this particular case -- in this particular case the Prosecutor, after submitting a request for investigation to be conducted, halted that investigation and gave a proposal to the investigative judge to suspend further proceedings in this case which was done in May of 1993. So in every case where I had information indicating that there was a decision by the public prosecutor pursuant to a criminal report, I inserted the data into the table. Where you see blanks, that means that there was no decision taken either vis-a-vis the indictment or if the indictment was issued there was no judgement by the court. So whenever I had information, whenever I had files, I inserted data from the files into these columns.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just for the record, she was referring to the entry that's -- involves case that has a KT number of 157/92. Let's turn the page to page 37 of the B/C/S and page 19 of the English. And this is issue 3 which is the statistical data you collected regarding the criminal reports received by the prosecutor's office, in this case the Teslic prosecutor's office between 1 April and 31 December 1992. I just want to clarify just two things for us with regard to this data. First, we see under the first two entries you provide the total number of criminal charges recorded in the KT and KTN log-books. What do you mean by criminal charges?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: When we look at table 3, I inserted in table 3 all cases which reached the basic prosecutor's office in Teslic between the 1st of April, 1992, until the 31st of December, 1992. When I put a total number of criminal reports, I -- the ones that came from the KT log-book, I included all criminal reports which were entered into the KT log-book against perpetrators who were of age. So KT log-book is a registry book for criminal reports against perpetrators of age. Now, whether these reports were filed by authorised officials, that is to say police, or SJBs or citizens or other entities is irrelevant. What is important for the KT log-book is that the perpetrator's identity is known.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, and I want to clarify just one particular point, and I think you've addressed it. But these total numbers that you provide in the first two entries here, are they the number of criminal reports, the number of cases, or are they the number of perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: In column number 1, I inserted a total number of criminal reports, regardless of the number of perpetrators. It could be that there were many more perpetrators here. I simply looked at the number of criminal reports in the period between the 1st of April, 1992, and 31st of December, 1992; number of reports filed with the basic prosecutor's office in Teslic regarding known perpetrators, regardless of the number of perpetrators. This just reflects the number of criminal reports filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the rest of the data that is contained in this table beginning with the number of indictments and continuing down, is this data from the KT log-book or does it also include data from the KTN log-books?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: In column 2 underneath the KT log-book, I inserted there the total number of criminal reports in the KTN log-book with the basic prosecutor's office in Teslic, and that was 12 within the same period of time. So number 12 -- the figure of 12 reflects the number of criminal reports filed against unknown perpetrators. Then I put in the number of indictments issued which was 64. I also counted cases and not perpetrators, and then further down the data that you see in table 3, all of it reflects cases and not perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And we understand that, but the clarification I want to make is we see first 64 indictments and then we see the number of criminal reports for various crimes. Were those derived from the KT log-book, the rest of the data on this chart?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. From the KT log-book, that is to say against known perpetrators. Only figure from column 2 pertains to unknown perpetrators, whereas the rest of the data pertains to known perpetrators and I took this information from the KT log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to issue 4, which is page 38 of the B/C/S and page 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. Before we leave this schedule. First of all, Madam, I have a question to you regarding the number of perpetrators. Is that included in this chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this table you can see the following. Let's focus on one or two issues. Total number of cases, in cases of war crimes and crimes against humanity, based on this wording you can see that this pertains only to known perpetrators. I wrote down the number of criminal reports regardless of whether there was one perpetrator or five perpetrators, because those were my instructions. All of this pertains to known perpetrators of crimes and the list of crimes is given below. This is in the period between the 1st of April, 1992, until the 31st of December, 1992. Whatever was entered into the KT log-book with the basic public prosecutor's office in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand, but my question was really if it is possible to extract from this chart how many perpetrators were involved, because if you look at the first entry on top of the chart you see the total number of criminal charges recorded in the KT log-book, and the figure says 132 charges. Now, I suppose that several charges might be raised against one perpetrator. So my question was: How many perpetrators are involved in this chart? Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, there might be a slight problem with the translation, Your Honours, because the Serbian says "krivicna prijava," which is a criminal report or criminal complaint filed with the office of the public prosecutor. So it's not the criminal charges, it's the number of criminal reports which were filed with the prosecutor -- with the prosecutor's office. I don't know if I was of assistance. I thought maybe that is maybe creating the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Zecevic, for this clarification, and that is indeed an important point that you are raising. Nevertheless, I sit back with the question of how many perpetrators were involved in the number of criminal reports, the 132 criminal reports that were registered in the KT log-book. Because my assumption would be that it probably includes a considerably smaller number of perpetrators because the reports would -- or maybe bigger. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the very outset I said that in table 3 I counted only reports, not perpetrators of crimes. However, sometimes in one single report there are several perpetrators listed. I only counted the number of criminal reports, regardless of the number of perpetrators; I did not enter information on perpetrators, how many perpetrators were involved in each particular crime. It could be that from -- for the crime in Articles 36 to 38 I listed down four criminal reports, that is to say four cases. It could be that there were ten perpetrators involved. So I put down information concerning criminal reports, not perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. And with the clarification that Counsel Zecevic provided, it would seem that the number of perpetrators would for sure exceed the number of 132. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible, given that my instruction was to go by cases. As a result of that, I did not analyse perpetrators. It could be done subsequently to see how many perpetrators there were and how many perpetrators were recorded in the KT log-book. It should be no problem to obtain that piece of information. I looked at cases, not perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question goes to the penultimate entry which seems to be a bit vague to me. I simply don't understand what it comprises. It reads: "The total number of serving with the enemy army cases against non-Serb perpetrators under Article 119." What does this cover, Madam, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I may be of assistance again. I believe the translation again is a problem. Maybe Your Honours can invite the -- our interpreters to read the penultimate paragraph of the chart and I will -- I'm sure you will better understand what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't know if the translators have the text in B/C/S, but if not then could you please read it out, Mr. Zecevic, or Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just -- just for the record, I think Your Honour's referring to the -- not the -- yeah, the penultimate one, yes. Why don't we have the witness read it out since she has it in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Ms. Gacinovic, can you read the second-to-last entry on this chart.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: In the penultimate line it says: "Total number of cases for the crime of serving in the enemy army Article 119 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY." So this is not a crime committed against non-Serb individuals. My task was to list the number of criminal reports in the given period from the 1st of April, 1992, until the 31st of December for the crime of serving in the enemy army, Article 119 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, where the perpetrators were of non-Serb ethnicity, that is to say Muslims or Croats. So the same of the crime is serving in the enemy army, Article 119 of the Criminal Code. It wasn't my job to see how many criminal reports were filed for this crime, no. My job was to see how many perpetrators were reported for the crime of serving in the enemy army, Article 119, where the perpetrators were non-Serbs, that is to say Muslims, Croats, or of some other ethnicity. Perhaps it was confusing for you that it says here serving with the enemy army cases against non-Serb perpetrators under Article 119, perhaps the word order should have been different in order to make it more clear for you. My job, however, was to establish how many were reported for Article 119 where the perpetrators were of non-Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, and I admit it was indeed confusing. But, Madam, let me be clear, what are we talking about here? Are we talking about charges raised against Muslims for serving in the Muslim army? Is that what is included in this entry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This reflects the today number of cases that arrived at the prosecutor's office during this period of time for this particular crime. We have no information as to any indictments or the resolution of the case. In cases where there were indictments, that's reflected in the column for indictments. As far as I can remember, I don't think that a single indictment was issued for this particular crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. But that's not the issue. My question to you is: Were criminal charges brought against Muslims for serving in the Muslim army during the time covered by this chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't enter that -- such information in this table. I only did what I was instructed to do. It was my duty to mention only the number of indictments issued, regardless of the crime committed. I didn't state the number of indictment by individual criminal reports. I only listed the total number of criminal reports from April till December 1992, but I didn't make a breakdown to the type of criminal offence because that wasn't my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe if I can intervene here and help clarify matters. Her job was to only look at the log-books. Now, log-books, as you've seen already, they list the perpetrators, the victims, and the procedure that the case went through; it doesn't give the facts of the case. So she identified cases of criminal reports filed against non-Serbs for serving in the enemy army. Now, what enemy army they were serving in, you're not going to get that from the log-books. You would have to pull the criminal file and see what's actually alleged. The criminal report would say they were, for instance, with the Green Berets or they were with the BiH army or what have you. But from the log-books which is what she reviewed, she wouldn't be able to tell you which enemy army they were serving with, because her scope was really just limited mainly to log-books, and then we referred to some cases -- case files where it fell under issue number 1 or 2, or you'll see number 4 to get clarification to make sure that they fall under one of those issues. But for the statistical purpose, all she did is go through the log-books is say, Yes this is an enemy army case, and yes, it's charging non-Serb perpetrators so that's one. And then find another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I'm sorry. You can't help asking the question of what does this actually signify? What lies behind these entries? I am fully aware of the fact that this is just a statistical review, but nevertheless the witness is a prosecutor and I would assume you would be able to tell us what does this penultimate entry cover. And to your knowledge were charges brought? Apparently there were 15 charges registered against non-Serb persons for serving in the enemy army, and this looks mysterious to me. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Thank you very much, Madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just provide some clarification? I only adhered to the table, only what was mentioned in the table, and I entered the relevant information from the log-books. I entered the total number of indictments, regardless of the criminal -- underlying criminal offence. And I relied only on the number of criminal reports filed. Let's take as an example Article 119 of the Criminal Code. I proceeded the same way with regard to Article 116. So I strictly adhered to the requirements of this table and didn't pay attention to the ethnicity -- to issues such as ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, you may want to refer to the testimony of ST-176 to get further clarification regarding the nature of these cases in Teslic and the reasons for them being filed and other information that perhaps Your Honours are seeking with regard to the particular cases here. If we may turn to page 38 of the original as well as page 20 of the English, this is issue 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Which is where you recorded entries that you identified in the log-books which you required additional information to determine whether they fell either under one of the indictment's schedules or involved serious crimes against non-Serbs. Now, turning to the first couple entries, the KTN entries that you recorded under issue 4, and this applies generally to your other tables for -- under issue 4, did you find any indication in any of the log-books that a criminal report was ever filed against a known perpetrator for these particular crimes that you identify under issue 4?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: By reviewing the KTN and KTA log-books, I didn't find information showing that the perpetrator of these crimes was identified nor that criminal reports were filed with the basic prosecutor's office in Teslic for these crimes on the dates of the 13th -- or rather, committed on the 13th and 14th of November and the 15th of September and so on. One would have to check the records of the basic public prosecutor's office in Teslic to find the relevant information. That's why I entered these in table 4 because they require additional documentation to complete this review.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to clarify, these entries -- these KTN entries that you record under issue number 4, those are not found in the KT log-book because if they were found in the KT log-book you would have recorded that in entry under issue number 2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: By reviewing the log-books, I found in some cases that the perpetrator of a crime was identified and then I entered a remark that he was identified and that the case was entered under certain item number in a log-book because I wanted to establish a link between unidentified and identified perpetrators but I wasn't able to do so for these four cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the KTA entries that you have recorded here under issue number 4, we see that they reference the basic court. What was the basic court submitting to the prosecutor's offices or the prosecutor's office of Teslic in this instance?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: It follows from this table that the investigative judge of the basic court in Teslic conducted an on-site investigation on the occasion of a murder that happened on the 15th of September, 1992, at Banja Vrucica and on the 22nd of September, 1992, at Osovica. He drafted an on-site investigation report and submitted it with the public prosecutor's office in Teslic under the file numbers as stated in the table. The investigative judge makes an on-site investigation report and submits it to the public prosecutor's office and copies the police station on it because the police assists in the on-site investigation, that is, the authorised officials from the police station who make a file including photographs, sketches, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if subsequently the police file a criminal report against a known or unknown perpetrator for one of these cases that you refer to in the KTA, where would that case be transferred to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: If the police submits the remaining documentation that was made at the site, in this case it is added to the case file. In this concrete case of murder, the whole file is entered in the KT log-book and this file which is entered in the KTA log-book is entered in the log-book that contains identified or known perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And am I correct in stating that if the police file a criminal report against an unknown perpetrator on that -- that this case would then transfer from the KTA into the KTN log-book?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If the police file a criminal report against an unidentified perpetrator and after the on-site investigation the police fails to identify the perpetrator, then the police file a criminal report against an unknown perpetrator with the public prosecutor's office. Since the police already have the on-site investigation report, or rather, the public prosecutor does, the case is entered in the KTN log-book. And what was received from the court is also entered in the KTN log-book together with what was received from the police and the two files are merged because they refer to one and the same offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Oh, I was pleased to hear you say "finally." I was just about to point out to you that you're ten minutes past your 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise. I just want to now go over some general trend issues that I think might be helpful for the Trial Chamber. I don't think it's going to take long.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I just want to ask you some questions about some of the general trends you observed from your review of the prosecutor's log-books for the period of 1992 to 1995. First, did the log-books indicate to you that the district and basic prosecutor's offices in the various municipalities were functioning in 1992 and subsequently?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by reviewing all log-books that I received when I worked on this project, in the time-period from the 1st of April until the end of 1992 I saw that occasionally there were criminal reports against identified or unidentified perpetrators and the public prosecutor's office worked on these cases and so did the courts in that period because there are court decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the prosecutor offices that you worked for in Trebinje in 1992 and subsequently, were your -- was your office able to receive and process criminal cases during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That can be seen from the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, based on your review, what can you tell us about the number of criminal cases or criminal reports filed with the prosecutor's offices in 1993 or 1994 or 1995 that relate to crimes that were committed in 1992? What can you tell us about the overall number of those? Were there many of those?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Not many. Criminal reports for offences committed in 1992 were mostly filed during that same year, although some of them were filed later but there weren't many such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We propose to take the adjournment now, but only for 15 minutes, at which point, Mr. Zecevic, we would ask you to report to us how much -- at what point you would comfortably be in a position to begin your cross-examination. So we return in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I informed Ms. Featherstone and Ms. Audrey about the -- what we are suggesting at the moment as a way how to proceed. What I proposed and what I'm prepared to do at this point is -- the fact is that my cross-examination concerns two particular points actually in general. One is the general position of the office of the prosecutor and the police according to the laws at the time, and I'm ready to start with this general points in the cross-examination. And I propose to lead -- to cross-examine the witness on these points up until I believe one hour and a half. And then that we are adjourned and I have half an hour to 45 minutes tomorrow after I reviewed the -- and analysed additional statement which was given to us last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I understand that. I would ask the court officer to work out at what time we should take the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so could the witness -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. Gacinovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will put several questions to you regarding your testimony earlier today. Today at page 9 of the transcript, line 21, when asked by Mr. Olmsted whether you could confirm, given the revisions to the annex, that the information contained in your written statements was correct and accurate you said yes. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the statement that you gave yesterday, the revised statement of the 27th and 28th September was drafted in English; right -- just please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I want to answer. Yesterday when we worked in proofing, the statement was read out loud to me, we compared the tables, and I could confirm that what was written in the statement was indeed what I wanted to state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: And I also compared it with the tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: A bit, not really well but I do speak some.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your statement drafted yesterday, the first 15 pages is in English; right? You signed that statement. Did you read it in English or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: As I told you, I read out some of it myself in English, but in addition to that the interpreter read it out loud to me in my language and I confirmed that. And then I put my signature and date to it, and I compared the data that I had with what was written in the tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. So the statement was read out to you by an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in my presence; and to the extent that I was able, I read the statement myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you for the sake of interpretation to please make pauses between my question and your answer.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, today Mr. Olmsted showed to you the document from Teslic, and while it is still fresh in our minds let us discuss it. That's 65 ter 10530, and the page that was shown to the witness pertains to the revised annex number 9 to Teslic, to municipality of Teslic, and the prosecutor's office in Teslic. I really can't remember what page number it was. I think it was page 32. I think that's the page I need in English. It was issue number 3. Perhaps it was page 34. I apologise for not being accurate enough, but I did not have occasion to look at the document or study it a bit. So that's why we're having these problems. Yes, that's the page. Can you see this? This is revised annex 9, issue number 3. Madam Gacinovic, the prosecutor's office has the following log-books: KT log-book for criminal reports against known perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: KTN for criminal reports against unknown perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: KTM for criminal reports against minors?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, known minors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: KTA for accompanying documentation such as on-site investigation reports, official records, and other documentation pertaining to certain events for which an indictment was not yet issued?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Teslic -- or rather, did you study the KTM log-book in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: As I said at the outset, I only checked KT, KTN, and KTA log-book, and you can see that reflected in table 1 where I stated that I checked log-books in Teslic for 1992 KT; and then KT for 1993, 1994, and 1995; and KTA for the same years. That is to say I did not check the log-books -- I did not check KTM log-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So concerning issue 3 of the revised annex 9, the prosecutor's office in Teslic had 132 criminal reports in the KT log-book, and then in KTN log-book there were 12 reports. Tell me, please, did some of the reports recorded in KTN log-book get transferred to the KT log-book in Teslic for the year of 1992, if you are aware of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: While working on issue number 3, I only analysed how many there were recorded reports in KT and KTN log-books during the relevant period of time. I did not analyse whether any of the reports were transferred from KTN to KT log-book. I strictly adhered to my instructions and to the task given to me. If there is a criminal report filed in the KTN log-book against an unknown perpetrator and then the perpetrator gets identified, that year or in the following five years there is a column where there should be an entry as to whether the file, the case, and the information was transferred to the KT log-book for perpetrators that are of age or into the KTM log-book for perpetrators that are minors. However, I did not look for that kind of information because I was not told to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order to clarify, there is a logical sequence in these log-books that are kept in the prosecutor's office. First of all, the first information that arrives about an event is recorded either in an official note or in a document called information or in the on-site investigation report. It is sent as such to the prosecutor's office and then recorded in the KTA log-book; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends. If an investigative judge goes to an on-site investigation together with authorised officials, whether the prosecutor is present or not the judge will draw up a report on the on-site investigation. The police will do the rest. They will take photographs and do other things that need to be done. Then the investigative judge draws up the on-site investigation report. This is how it was done during this period of time. This report is sent in two copies to the prosecutor's office, and then a copy or two are filed with the court and then also one copy is sent to the police station. This on-site report will be recorded by the prosecutor's office in the KTA log-book. Police continues its work and they will make photographs, they will collect statements from eye-witnesses, et cetera, and then together with the criminal report against the known perpetrator they will send it to the prosecutor's office. The prosecutor's office will record it in the KTA log-book with the proviso that the initial on-site investigation report that was received from the investigative judge will be transferred to the KT log-book. However, this will be reflected as an entry in the KTA log-book. If the police learns of something that happened but there was no need to conduct an on-site investigation, the police will draw up an official record and they may send it to the prosecutor's office. In the prosecutor's office they will record it in the KT [as interpreted] log-book, and then later on should a criminal report be filed then this will be transferred to the KT log-book or KTM log-book or perhaps even KTN log-book. This is a piece of information indicating that something had happened and that something is being done about it. The on-site investigation report is drawn up only when while conducting an on-site investigation they come to a conclusion that indeed a crime had been perpetrated and then they will -- they would draw up an on-site investigation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just -- I'm sorry, just to clarify. In the record, page 30, line 19, she says that the official note would be recorded in the KT log-book. I believe that she most likely meant the KTA log-book. Maybe you want to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it should be KTA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, all of us here are attempting to be of assistance to the Trial Chamber. So please focus on my questions and give us brief answers because I don't think that what we have just done was of assistance to the Trial Chamber. Your answer was fully correct, but it was overly broad and you provided too much information in one answer.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the witness, as the speakers overlapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think it would be best if we could explain this using an example. Let's say a body is found, a corpse. And then an official record is drawn up or a report from the on-site investigation, and then this document is sent to the prosecutor's office as a piece of information on the event that had happened. So this document would be recorded in the KTA log-book; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Following a forensic examination, for example, of a forensic expert, it is established that this was a case of natural death. The corpse's identity is provided and this is where any further activity on the prosecutor's office halts; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. No need to do anything else except to inform the family that there are no grounds for criminal prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is requested to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the prosecutor's office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The interpreters are reminding the witness to speak into the microphone, and while the -- I would remind the witness of what counsel's already alerted her to, that to allow a gap between the question and the answer so there's no overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would also kindly request Mr. Zecevic to switch off his microphone when the witness is answering because she's very difficult to hear when both microphones are switched on. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Noted. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in case a dead body is found, the public prosecutor's office is informed by the services and agencies in charge. It is entered in the KT A log-book, and if it is established that there are no elements of a criminal offence it stays in the KTA log-book and the public prosecutor's office is informed accordingly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: There is no need to take any official action in such a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If in such a situation after a forensic analysis it is established that this was a case of violent death, after certain additional activity is conducted by the police, a criminal report against an unknown perpetrator is filed; correct? And then the event entered in the KTA log-book is transferred to the KTN log-book; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Once that event was transferred to the KTN log-book after a certain time -- and after a certain time the perpetrator of the crime is found or identified, then the police informs the public prosecutor's office that they have established the identity of the perpetrator or the suspect, then the entry is transferred from the KTN log-book to the KT log-book; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were -- some things were unclear, so we should assist the Trial Chamber. Concerning criminal offence 172 and 177 or under -- that fall under Articles 172 and 177 of the Criminal Code of SFRY -- or rather, the SR BiH, the -- as regards the differences between Articles 172 and 177 of the Criminal Code of the S R BiH is that Article 177, which you say you relied on, describes a criminal offence with a -- with serious consequences; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the so-called elements of the crime are identical in Article 172 and Article 177 only that serious consequences are included in Article 177. So that is the specific difference that makes a criminal offence come under Article 177; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what I explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted on page 12 of today's transcript, line 14 and 24, showed to you KT 177 [as interpreted] from 1992 against one Mile Stanojevic. That's the revised appendix 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Appendix 9, issue 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify again for the record, I believe under issue 2 this is KT 157/92. I think she misspoke when she said 177.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, 157/92.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it, Madam?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The question my learned friend asked you was about the last entry in the table where it says that the investigation was suspended on 12 May 1993, and the document is self-explanatory in this sense. If the perpetrator of a crime dies, we're talking about an identified person whose name is Mile Stanojevic, so this Mile Stanojevic commits a crime, a criminal report is filed, but the investigation was suspended in 1993. I'm interested in the following: Is the investigation suspended when the accused or the suspect dies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: The investigation is suspended. I didn't review the case file. I just collected information from the log-books which showed that a criminal report was filed against Mile Stanojevic, that the injured party was Fadil, that the offence was committed on 5 August 1992, and that the criminal charges were brought under Article 148, paragraph 1. But I don't have information about the reasons why the investigation was suspended. If I had had the case file, I could have answered your question. An investigation is suspended when the public prosecutor makes a proposal to the investigating judge to suspend the investigation. Possible reasons are the death of the perpetrators or that the suspect did not commit the offence, but that's information I didn't have. However, this column reads only investigation suspended and the relevant date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to clarify. Let us return to revised annex 9, issue 3. If I remember correctly, that's page 34 of this document. That's the previous document that we saw. We can see from this overview of statistical data that between April and 31st of December, 1992, the basic public prosecutor's office in Teslic received a total of 144 criminal reports. That is 132 against known perpetrators and 12 against unknown perpetrators; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But your reservation was that it was possible that a certain number of criminal reports was filed against perpetrators who are minors, but since you did not review the relevant log-books you couldn't say any more about that; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not review KTM log-books. Whatever I say would be my assumptions, but I'm not supposed to assume. I can only speak about what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that a short answer to my question will be yes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: There are minor offenders anywhere, so we can assume as much, but it wouldn't be fair to state anything based on assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But I repeat, the answer to my question is yes. You did not review KTM log-books and that is why it is possible that there is a number of reports against minor perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot comment because I did not consult the KTM log-books, so -- which are for minor perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You explained here that your statistics are based on the number of criminal reports. I believe that you explained, but for the sake of complete clarity of the transcript let me summarise that one criminal report can be filed against a greater number of perpetrators; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So a criminal report can be filed against one perpetrator, but also for 50 perpetrators in the same case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us reconfirm. One criminal report can be filed against one perpetrator for several offences, that is either one offence or several; and likewise, it can be filed against several perpetrators for one offence or several offences; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, to be totally complete, several criminal reports can be filed against one and the same perpetrator; is that right, Madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But when several criminal reports are filed against one and the same perpetrator, then each criminal report is for a different offence; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: It can be the same criminal offence, but it can be about several offences. It all depends on what the perpetrator has done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know. But if, for example, Petar Petrovic is the suspect for murder and one criminal report is filed against him for murder and the public prosecutor's office receives another criminal report against the same person for the same offence, then you wouldn't enter both criminal reports but only one; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: The first criminal report is entered under one item number, and if another report comes in against the same person for the same offence it is entered in the case file, the same file.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if one criminal report is already filed against one perpetrator for one offence, all possible subsequent criminal reports for the same offence against the same perpetrator would become part of the same case file; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: If it's the very same event, yes. But if we're talking about different events, then it all depends on the -- on the stage of the procedure in which the previous case is at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that one more thing remained insufficiently clear. I'm referring to page 22, I believe, where there was discussion about criminal offences under Article 119 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY and that is serving in an enemy army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show us 65 ter 10130, that's tab 159 of the Defence binder. While we're waiting, I need Article 119. The page reference is 60 and the ERN number is 0025-3452.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to appear, Madam, it's a fact that the RS took over the Criminal Code of the SFRY; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you know, tell me, isn't it true that the Criminal Code of the SFRY was also applied in the territories controlled by the Muslim and Croat forces, which is the territory of nowadays Federation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know which laws and regulations they took over. I know how we went about it in the RS, which laws we took over and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We see Article 119 here, which describes the criminal offence of serving in an enemy army; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know whether the courts and prosecutor's offices in the Federation submitted criminal reports against citizens of Serbian ethnicity under the same article, namely for their belonging to the RS army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To clarify for the benefit of the Court the documents that get entered into K TA log-book, let me show to you two documents from Doboj. The first one is 1D01-0315, tab 157. As you can see, Madam, this is a memo by the security services centre Doboj. The date is the 25th of August, 1992. The document is signed by the chief of the centre, Andrija Bjelosevic. This is an accompanying letter and it is stated that it's -- that attached is the on-site investigation report and the interview of the witnesses. The prosecutor's office in Doboj is informed about a certain event, namely, that an anti-tank mine was blown off which resulted in death of Hodzic Sejfudin. A driver Bozidar Vidovic received injuries. There were some other people injured as well. The injured parties are people of both Muslim and Serb ethnicity; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This type of document would normally be entered into the KTA log-book of the prosecutor's office; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In essence, the prosecutor's office on the basis of such a memo received by the CSB, the prosecutor's office has information about the event only; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, unless there are any objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm not sure why it's particularly relevant to this case. I mean, the witness doesn't know anything about this particular event and I think he's shown it to another witness and basically the witness is giving the same general answers about procedures. I think the procedure is established; the relevance of the document itself is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, what -- how does this document assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, the position of the Defence is that the work of the police is completed at the moment when documents concerning a certain event is submitted to the relevant prosecutor's office, and the purpose of tendering this document was to show an example of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I thought that we were exploring reports relating to Article 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believed, Your Honours, that it was sufficient to have shown the SFRY Criminal Code, where one could find an explanation as to substance of a crime under Article 119. I don't have any other interest here except by using the assistance of the witness to explain the situation. But if you wish me to do so we can go and elaborate it to the smallest details, but I move to a different topic really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I missed that and I apologise for that. I thought actually that this memo from Doboj was supposed to illustrate one of the 15 reports that were --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- included in the schedule put together by the witness. But if that is not the case, then what is it that you seek to show with this memo?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in accordance with Rule 90(H), this document would be relevant for the Defence case. Through the assistance of the witness, I'm attempting to enter a document as an illustration of the fact that the CSB reports basic public prosecutor's office in charge of the territory in question about events. The question here is whether this case was transferred either to the KT or the KTN log-books because what we have here is a case of an anti-tank mine. A vehicle hit the mine and one person got killed and several -- or all together three persons were injured. So I believe that in that sense it's relevant for our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has identified this case in her annexes, so the fact that this particular event occurred or this document was filed with the prosecutor's office is in her annexes under I believe it's KTA 74/92. Now, if the Defence is claiming that this case resulted in eventually the police filing a criminal report, then they should produce the criminal report of that. The fact that it is in her report under issue number 4, she's indicated that implies that there was no criminal report filed in that matter -- or at least the log-books did not indicate that a criminal report was filed for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What I was going to ask is whether in terms of the procedure, which as I understand it was the purpose of your seeking to tender this in support of the -- what you are showing the procedure to be, isn't it sufficient that we have the testimony of this witness and other witnesses in that regard and the illustration of this particular incident notwithstanding its being cross-referenced in the annexes to the present witness's report. It doesn't advance the clarity of the matter for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my idea precisely was to show by giving you an example, to show you something that both this witness and some other witnesses demonstrated, namely, that such an event could be found logged in the KTA log-book. I just wanted to help the Trial Chamber see what this was really about. In the KTA log-book you can only find several details and numbers, but if you believe all this is superfluous I will not insist and ask for tendering this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The Prosecution doesn't dispute that this case -- that this document or at least this event was recorded in the KTA log-book for Doboj. As I indicated, it's in her annex, and therefore if it's in her annex, the Prosecution will agree that the prosecution receives something from the police with regard to this case. In this case it was just an Official Note about an event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely the essence of this, Your Honours. This is the essence. Tomorrow the Prosecutor will say in their final argument that the police informed the prosecutor's office about this event, that the event was entered into the KTA log-book, and then police stopped taking any actions in relation to this case. This is why I'm using this specific example, showing that there was nothing to do. How can police determine where did the anti-tank mine come from, who placed it, and so forth? Well, it is possible to do so, but that would involve enormous resources and take a lot of time. That is the essence of our case here, namely, in showing you specific examples and documents related to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'll agree with -- Your Honours, I'll agree with Mr. Zecevic's statement that to find out whether this was a crime it would require the police to do further investigation. I think that's obvious. But I ask that Mr. Zecevic again refrain from characterising the Prosecution's case, particularly in front of a witness, because I don't think he knows necessarily our case inside and out and what our arguments eventually will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think we can move on. It still seems to me that the narrative of the events that forms the indictment in this trial, that something like this is at best a footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, the KTA log-books, what was entered into them was not only the Official Notes by the internal affairs organs nor only on-site investigation reports, it also included information the prosecutor's office received from citizens in regard to certain events; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The public prosecutor's office, they -- there are two main documents regulating it, one is the Criminal Code and the other one is the Law on Public Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Law of Code of Criminal Procedure and the Law of Public Prosecutors, but there were other laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. You will agree with me that the Law on Criminal Proceeding in Article 17 provided for the criminal procedure to be initiated upon the request of the public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: For such crimes that are dealt with ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And for other crimes, it was the injured party who could be the party that launches the proceedings; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: I believe in such cases one would file a private lawsuit, if I remember it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree that this was called private criminal complaint, but this kind of document, complaint or lawsuit, would rather be the first stage of the criminal proceeding?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: But that was independent of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Independently in relation to the public prosecutor; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that the Law on Criminal Proceeding in Articles 45 to 51 devotes one whole chapter to public prosecutor; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember the provisions, yes. It's been a while since I've used that law so I may be wrong in giving you answers about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will remember just general postulates from the provisions where in Article 45 it was prescribed that the public prosecutor is in charge of crimes that are dealt with ex officio, including taking measures in determining the crime, finding the perpetrator, and directing the pre-trial criminal proceeding; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: You skipped paragraph 1 where you're saying that basic rights and duties of public prosecutor is to prosecute those crimes that are dealt with ex officio. You read paragraph 2, but you skipped paragraph 1 where it is stated that the basic task of the public prosecutor is to prosecute those crimes that are prosecuted ex officio. I do not have the law before me, so I cannot give you a full interpretation. You have it so you can confirm it. And in paragraph 2, yes, what you just read that's what is stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, Madam. Your memory serves you right when it comes to these regulations. What I read out to you, paragraph 2, item 1, because I want to ask you the following question or a question. So we agree that the public prosecutor under paragraph 1, item -- paragraph 2, item 1 takes necessary action to detect crimes and identify perpetrators and take measures to direct the pre-trial criminal proceedings. Could you please explain the meaning of this formulation in the law directing the pre-trial criminal proceedings, but very briefly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: It depends on a case. Once the prosecutor informs what he has available and what he needs to obtain what the organs of the interior need to do, what kind of steps they need to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which means when the prosecutor receives information or criminal report, then he, according to the law, directs and indicates the direction in which certain facts should be established by the organs of the interior, i.e., the police; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In many cases that's how it is and in many other cases the police itself once it learns that a crime was committed does it on its own because this is their duty under the law. Once a crime is committed for which persecution needs to take place under the law, then the police is duty-bound to take certain steps. And I think that this is regulated by Article 151. The police is duty-bound to do certain steps, regardless of the steps taken by the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, if the police takes all these steps and they don't provide expected results, then the prosecutor can direct the police to do certain other steps, to conduct other checks, or obtain some other evidence. The prosecutor is entitled to do that; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: I can give you a very brief explanation. Once a criminal report is filed against an unknown perpetrator, the police until that time has done everything it was able to do. And then it sends the report to the prosecutor against unknown perpetrator.
