The last sentence in every criminal report reads that in addition to everything that is enclosed with that report, the police will continue working on establishing the identity of the perpetrator. And if they manage to do that, then they will send a criminal report against the known perpetrator. However, if something else was recorded in the KTA log-book and the prosecutor while working on the case believes that police or somebody else needs to take additional steps, then the prosecutor can direct them to go and collect statements or conduct other steps. This is the kind of direction that the prosecutor can give in pre-trial proceedings to the police. However, if the prosecutor establishes that the police has done everything it was able to do until that point in time, then there is no need for them to do anything else and they can perhaps have a phone call and conclude that the police has done everything it was able to do in that particular case until that time. It just all depends on the particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When the prosecutor's office conducts work on a certain case, when they're working on collecting evidence that would enable the prosecutor to draft the indictment properly and to have sufficient evidence to support the indictment, then the prosecutor gives certain instructions or sends requests to police to obtain certain evidence, such as to carry out a forensic analysis or additional forensic analysis or to carry out a ballistic examination or something of that kind; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: I have already explained this. If the prosecutor establishes that something else is needed in the file, then he can ask that additional statements be obtained or other additional steps be taken, and this comes all under Article 152 of the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you said Article 153, paragraph 2, and the transcript reflects Article 152.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. As far as I can remember, I think it's Article 153, paragraph 2. Perhaps my memory is not what it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, you're absolutely right. It's 153, paragraph 2. However, paragraph 3 of that same article of the Law on Criminal Procedure says as follows and gives the following authorisation to the prosecutor. It says: "Public prosecutor can seek the necessary information from state organs, from organisations of associated labour, other organisations and associations, and can also for that purpose send a request to the person who submitted the relevant criminal report." Right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of that is fully correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in accordance with the role of the public prosecutor, as defined by the constitution and the law, all of these state organs, all of the individuals and organisations were duty-bound to act pursuant to the request sent out by the public prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If they were able to act upon the request of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will remind you of Article 16 which says that: "The public prosecutor's office is entitled to receive from courts and other organs and entities all documents and information that are necessary for the public prosecutor to act within its competence." The last paragraph says that: "Organs and individuals from paragraphs 1 and 2 of this article are duty-bound to act pursuant to the requests sent out by the prosecutor."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I said Article 16 I failed to say that I was referring to the law on public prosecutor's office, and the law on public prosecutor's office is 1D04-2985. Unfortunately we are still missing the translation of this law, but as soon as we have the translation we will file it into our law library and we have already agreed on this with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While you are paused, Mr. Zecevic, the hour and a half you indicated would run until noon, but in any event for the usual technical reasons we cannot sit beyond 12.10 so that you would indicate around noon whether we should come back after usual break or whether at that point we will take the adjournment until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can give you my answer right now. I'm going to lead the cross-examination until noon and then I propose that we adjourn for tomorrow and I will finish the rest of my cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us go back once again to the Law on Criminal Procedure. Just a minute. I need to find it. That's P120, tab 152. No need to show it on the screen. I just want your comment, please. It seems that you have very good memory of the Law on Criminal Procedure which was in force at the time. Since you have mentioned the case of -- or rather, the case of unknown perpetrators, I would like to remind you of Article 152 -- 155 of the Law on Criminal Procedure, which envisioned that: "In cases when the perpetrator is unknown, public prosecutor can request from the organs of the interior to take certain investigative steps should that be deemed useful and that they can ask for this even before an investigation is initiated." Further on: "If the public prosecutor believes that an investigative judge needs to take certain steps or if he believes that an autopsy or exhumation of a corpse needs to be conducted, the prosecutor will -- shall propose to the investigative judge to do that." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure, the investigative judge could disagree with the proposal advanced by the public prosecutor, proposal to conduct such investigative action?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: He could disagree with the request of the public prosecutor to launch an investigation. Now you're talking about just investigative step. I'm not sure whether he could disagree with the request to conduct certain investigative steps. I'm not entirely sure of that. When it comes to initiating an investigation, then I'm sure that you're right; but when it comes to just certain investigative steps, I'm not fully sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will read you, this is Article 155, paragraph 1, the last sentence. This is the Law on Criminal Procedure of the SFRY. So the last sentence reads: "If the investigative judge disagrees with this proposal, he shall request that the chamber rule on this."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to an investigation or just individual investigative steps?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, please focus. Article 155 reads, let me read it in its entirety: "If the public prosecutor believes that certain investigative steps need to be taken by the investigative judge or if there is a need to perform an autopsy or exhumation of a corpse, the public prosecutor shall propose to the investigative judge to undertake that step. If the investigative judge disagrees with that proposal, then he will request that a chamber rule on it." In parenthesis it says: "Article 23, paragraph 6."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You are right I have forgotten about this, and as I told you I don't remember all of the articles of the old Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So a special Trial Chamber ruled in these situations according to the Law on Criminal Procedure, these situations when the prosecutor proposes to the investigative judge to do something and the judge disagrees with that proposal. In such cases, a special Trial Chamber comprising three judges would rule on this, make a final ruling on this proposal of the prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly about the structure of the prosecutor's office. That's where we will conclude for today. I'm referring now to 1992 because that's the year that's relevant for this case. The structure of the prosecutor's office was as follows. There was a republic public prosecutor at the level of the republic, then there were district public prosecutors that worked with the district courts in their jurisdiction, and then there were first-instance or basic prosecutors that worked within the jurisdiction of the basic courts in the territory of the republic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 and I think to this day as well, there is a very clear hierarchy in the office of the prosecutor. The republic prosecutor is at the top, and then below him we have district prosecutors or higher prosecutors, and then basic prosecutors at the -- basic or junior prosecutors at the lowest level; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Each of these three prosecutor's offices had an identical internal organisation. At the head of the prosecutor's office there is a public prosecutor who has one first deputy and then several additional deputies. That's how it was at the level of the republic, at the district level, and at the basic level; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: It depends on the size of the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it depends on the size of the prosecutor's office, you mean that it can happen that at the basic level, at the lowest level, they have just one prosecutor and one deputy and not several deputies. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's how it could be at the middle level or at the highest level. It just depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know it was a rare occasion where a republic prosecutor's office would only have one prosecutor and one deputy and not several deputies. Have you -- are you familiar with any such instance as -- because you said that you've been a prosecutor since 1976 or so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned the years 1992 and 1993. And at that time I'm not sure whether there was only one prosecutor at the republic level or several, and whereas we at the district level in Trebinje -- there was one prosecutor, one deputy, and several second deputies. So it all depended on the resources and on needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 you were appointed senior prosecutor in Trebinje; correct ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992 it was called senior public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And your appointment, if I remember correctly, was in early August 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The higher prosecutor's office in Trebinje which was headed by you in 1992 had under its jurisdiction the basic prosecutor's offices in Trebinje, Ljubinje, Bileca, Gacko, Nevesinje, correct, Berkovici?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: You now mentioned the municipalities that were covered. There was a -- there was one higher prosecutor's office and three basic prosecutor's offices. There was Trebinje, Bileca, Gacko, Nevesinje, Berkovici. Actually, I'm not sure about Nevesinje. Possibly in the early days Nevesinje didn't have a basic prosecutor's office. I'm not sure when it was up and running, possible a couple of months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one question, if you remember. Was the jurisdiction of the public prosecutor's offices in Trebinje extended to cover the municipalities of Visegrad and Foca?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Foca belonged to Trebinje, but I don't think that Visegrad ever did. Trnovo did for a while, that municipality, together with Foca, Kalinovik, and Cajnice. But I don't think that Visegrad was ever under the jurisdiction of the Trebinje prosecutor's office as far as I remember. And Trnovo didn't remain under our jurisdiction for long either; it was soon transferred to Sarajevo. I'm not quite certain, but the CSB for a while had jurisdiction also over Foca and Visegrad, but that was soon changed; however, Foca in terms of the jurisdiction of the prosecutor's office there was under Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just have a few more questions and then we can finish. Article 17 of the Law on the Public Prosecutor's Office --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It's document 1D04-2985.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Article 17 explains the hierarchy within the public prosecutor's office, and it says: "The higher or senior public prosecutor," which was your position in 1992, "has the right and the duty to give binding instructions from work to the subordinate public prosecutor and in addition to that can conduct -- perform several activities from the jurisdiction of the junior public prosecutor. He can authorise the junior public prosecutor to act upon certain cases from the jurisdiction of the junior prosecutor, then he can authorise the junior public prosecutor to perform certain duties from the jurisdiction of another junior prosecutor." Let us clarify this. If you wish, I can give you a copy of the law for you to be able to control what I'm reading out.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: There is no need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you agree that this was the text that I read out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This basically means that the senior public prosecutor can order a junior public prosecutor, and let's assume that you are a senior prosecutor and there is a junior prosecutor in Bileca, let's say. And you can order him or give him binding instructions for his work or order him to perform certain activities; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As senior prosecutor, you also have the authority to -- I'm using "you" for the sake of argument. I don't want to insinuate anything. As senior prosecutor you can remove a case from a junior prosecutor and task another junior prosecutor to act on it or to deal with it; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only if there are reasons for that, not if it's a whim of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, certainly there must be reasons. If you're dissatisfied with their work, that is the work of one prosecutor, you can remove a case from them and transfer it to another and give instructions as to what should be done; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it didn't happen in our practice. It didn't happen, but it was possible under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in your personal practice it didn't happen, I suppose because you were satisfied with the work of your subordinate prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: I said that it didn't happen in our practice. There were only cases when the junior prosecutor or his deputy asked to be recused because they couldn't work on a certain case, and then I would task another prosecutor from our jurisdiction to deal with that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So let us shorten this. You as senior prosecutor have the authority to do what we have spoken about and which is provided for by Article 17, but you as senior prosecutor did not exercise your right -- that right in your practice or did so relatively rarely when the prosecutor himself would apply for -- to be recused?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And here's my last question: This same Article 17, paragraph 2, reads that: "The senior public prosecutor can take over criminal prosecution from the jurisdiction of a subordinate prosecutor ..." and it goes on to enumerate what the senior prosecutor is entitled to do. But the essence is that you as senior prosecutor, if you are dissatisfied with the work of any subordinate prosecutor, you have the authority to remove a case from their jurisdiction and decide to have the senior prosecutor's office to deal with that case; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since I will be moving to another unknown territory at the moment, I suppose we can take a break -- adjourn for the day and continue tomorrow. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. In my inquiries -- thank you, Mr. Zecevic, you may -- in my inquiries as to the -- how we were proceeding, I apologise that I neglected to inquire of counsel for Zupljanin as to how they were positioned to deal with cross-examination of this witness. But I advise that they are in a position to begin their cross-examination today, interposing in the cross-examination of Mr. Zecevic. Am I correctly advised, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since Mr. Zecevic have mostly covered what we wanted to deal with, we're basically left with only such matters as are included in the amendments. So we are not in a position to start our cross-examination today. So what will be left unresolved once Mr. Zecevic has finished will be dealt with us, but we would like to avoid going over the same things twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So in that case, we would take the adjournment until 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. Thank you. The -- Ms. Gacinovic, I would remind you that you, having been sworn as a witness, cannot have any contact with counsel from either side. You are excused for the day because we are about to take the adjournment as you would have gathered, to resume at 2.15 tomorrow. And in addition to such -- you're not being able to communicate with counsel, in such discussions as you may have with anyone else outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So with that we would rise and resume in this courtroom at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.
